en: [ACT II]
Same set. A few weeks later.
[SCENE I]
EUSTACHE, BÉATRICE, WERNER, GISELA : (Gisela is at the piano; Werner is preparing to sing.)

WERNER : That one, I'm sure you don't know it. It's a tiny one... no one ever sings it. It's a song from the Book of Suleika, by Goethe. (To Gisela.) Also ganz leise, bitte, Gisela. [So very softly, please, Gisela.] (He sings.) Wenn ich dein gedenke Fragt mich gleich der Schenke : Herr, warum so still? Da von deinen Lehren Immer weiter hören Saki gerne will. Wenn ich mich vergesse Unter der Zypresse, Hält er nichts davon; Und im stillen Kreise Bin ich doch so weise, Klug wie Salomon (1). [When I think of you, the cupbearer asks me at once: Master, why so silent? For Saki longs to hear more and more of your teachings. If I lose myself under the cypress tree, he thinks nothing of it; and yet in this quiet circle I am so wise, clever as Solomon.] (1) Hugo Wolf, Goethe-Lieder, IV, pp. 40-41.
BÉATRICE : It is exquisite... and that inflection... arriving right here on the B-flat chord...
WERNER, pleased. : Isn't it? I am glad that you noticed.
GISELA : But why don't you sing some Strauss instead?
WERNER : I don't like him.
BÉATRICE, to Eustache. : What do you say to it, Eustache?
EUSTACHE, dryly. : It seems pleasant to me.
WERNER : But how, pleasant? There is a form in it, a style; and yet that is the essential thing.
EUSTACHE : If you want my opinion, I find it morbid.
WERNER : How morbid? What do you mean?
EUSTACHE, growing heated. : In times like ours, one can no longer get passionate about these petty refinements.
WERNER, simply. : I don't understand.
EUSTACHE : We need music that speaks to the masses.
WERNER : You need trombones and tubas...
EUSTACHE : That kind of music addresses the idle; it is a superfluity. Art, as I conceive it, must be necessary.
WERNER, to Béatrice, laughing. : What he says is so funny.
EUSTACHE, stung. : I fail to see it.
WERNER : Mozart, for example—what do you think of Mozart?
EUSTACHE : Let's not go back over that old debate. I grant that there is probably something there that escapes me...
WERNER : You are still a bit proud of it all the same. (He bursts out laughing.)
EUSTACHE : I prefer to speak of what I like and what I am sure of appreciating.
WERNER : Perhaps even there you are mistaken.
GISELA : Werner!...
EUSTACHE : Beethoven...
WERNER : I was expecting that. But I fear there is a confusion here. You forgive Beethoven...
EUSTACHE, irritated. : I admire him.

WERNER : Because of the ideology. (He pronounces it with a hard "g".) That has nothing to do with music. Absolutely nothing. You think that music must provide fine thoughts. But it is not true. You also think that it is an instrument for... how do you say? zur Befreiung [for liberation].
BÉATRICE : Emancipation.
WERNER : It is not an instrument; it has its value in itself, a value greater than all ideas. I cannot explain, but I am certain.
EUSTACHE : At bottom, you are an advocate of art for art's sake. But that belongs to the past. If art is not integrated into collective life...
WERNER : What does that mean? You want to chain art, put it in service of the State, perhaps. You speak like a Hitlerite, nothing else.
EUSTACHE : Not on your life. But your individualism disgusts me, because it will always close its eyes to injustice, and feeds upon it.
WERNER : You are always speaking of injustices.
EUSTACHE : Well?
WERNER : What do you do against injustices? You go to meetings; you shout: Down with capitalism! Down with fascism! and God knows what else.
BÉATRICE, spiritedly. : You are not being fair, Werner; Eustache asks nothing better than to sacrifice himself for the good cause.
WERNER : What is the good cause?
BÉATRICE : You know very well that he will be in the front rank of those fighting for freedom the day it is threatened.
WERNER : But in the meantime? (Laughing.) I almost believe he would like to be in my place. But he can hardly have himself driven out just for the pleasure of being persecuted.
GISELA : What pleasure?

WERNER : Sometimes I think that you... how can one say? that you invent threats against yourselves that don't exist, simply to have the right to say: I am in danger, I am fighting, I am defending myself.
EUSTACHE : You people cannot understand anything about our situation.
WERNER : Naturally that is possible. Political parties in France are difficult...
EUSTACHE : If it pleases you to believe that social iniquity does not exist...

WERNER : It has always existed. Probably it always will exist. Mozart and Schubert were poor devils; sometimes they didn't know if they would have anything to eat. Still, they didn't say: I must compose revolutionary music.
EUSTACHE : Conscience has evolved since that time.
WERNER : What conscience?
EUSTACHE : There are abuses we will no longer tolerate.
WERNER : For ourselves or for others?
EUSTACHE : For others. If that isn't progress...
WERNER : I do not know. It is problematic. There have always been people who would not allow their neighbors to starve.
EUSTACHE : That is individual charity. That's a thing of the past.

WERNER : Yes, I know well, you believe in public assistance. As for me, I only think it is an office for spreading bad temper everywhere. There are people who say: if no one is satisfied, everyone will be a little pleased, because people will say to themselves: I am not well off, but my neighbor is not well off either. But I say: there may be no more misfortune perhaps, but there will be no joy either. Everyone will be in a bad temper. And that is the worst thing that can exist! With suffering one can still make music; not with bad temper.
EUSTACHE : Music! That is very secondary, after all.

WERNER : No, Eustache, it is not secondary. If music shrinks, if music becomes poorer, then life shrinks too, it becomes petty. Without music one no longer lives, one merely scrapes by... on vivote... do you say that in French?
EUSTACHE : You see everything as a musician. It's an occupational distortion.
WERNER : Possible. (A silence.) Would you like me to sing something else?
EUSTACHE : Unfortunately I have to go grade my papers. See you shortly. (He exits.)
[SCENE II]
GISELA : He's angry, it seems. You pay no attention to what you say. It's impolite.
WERNER : Politeness is for people one doesn't know. With a friend one must only say what one thinks... It is too important.
GISELA : Still, you don't have to hurt people's feelings.
WERNER : Music is all that remains...
BÉATRICE : It is sad for us, what you are saying.

WERNER : I only mean: music is a very great thing; politics is another thing, much less great, I think; that is my opinion in any case. But they cannot be mixed together. My poor dear Rudolf, he was a musician, he was also a communist: he was not a communist musician. A communist musician, das ist Unsinn, weiter nichts [that is nonsense, nothing more].
GISELA : That doesn't interest me. If politics has no importance, why didn't we stay in Germany? You chatter so much.
WERNER : It was not because of politics that I went away.
GISELA : Why then? Always Rudolf. And he is dead. It wasn't worth the trouble. You can't just ruin your whole life for someone who is beneath the ground.
WERNER : Please, Gisela!...
GISELA : It's too absurd. (To Béatrice.) I'm sure you agree.
BÉATRICE : I cannot allow myself to have an opinion; it is too grave. But I understand your husband.
GISELA : Well! I don't understand. (She stands up.) I am going to Paris now to buy that dress.
WERNER : What dress?
GISELA, losing patience. : I told you.
WERNER, laughing. : With what money will you pay for it?
GISELA, annoyed. : I still have something put aside.
WERNER : So much the better for you. (Gisela exits.)
[SCENE III]
WERNER, BÉATRICE : (Werner is smoking; his eyes are fixed on the door through which Gisela has just exited; he shakes his head with a smile.)

BÉATRICE, in an undertone. : Werner, I'm afraid you don't quite realize... (Werner turns his head toward her and looks at her questioningly.) Eustache is not happy; and... how should I say?... he needs others to understand him. Sometimes, without meaning to, I'm sure, you seem to try to put him in contradiction with himself, with his ideas... Yes, really; he feels that you are saying to yourself: "What is he complaining about? He has a secure position, a quiet life, not unpleasant at all..."
WERNER : It's true, though...

BÉATRICE : "Why does he want to turn everything upside down?" He senses you are thinking that, and let me tell you that it is unfair and dangerous. There is a trait in Eustache's character that seems very noble to me, and which even some of his comrades have not always known how to appreciate at its true worth... A thought that, I believe, has never left him.
WERNER : What thought?

BÉATRICE : "Just because I personally have been fortunate, because I have benefited from certain favorable circumstances, does not mean I will cease to think of those who haven't had the same luck, the same advantages. On the contrary. I will think of them more, always more. The more successful I am, the more I will cultivate indignation within myself." Why are you laughing, Werner?
WERNER : It is so funny to cultivate indignation like a vegetable... a prickly plant in any case. If you feel indignation you do not need to cultivate it, and if you do not feel it...
BÉATRICE : Eustache has an extremely scrupulous nature. It seems to him that a certain comfort, a certain ease, risks lulling the conscience to sleep.
WERNER : Conscience...
BÉATRICE, timidly. : Das Gewissen... [Conscience...]
WERNER : You don't need to translate. I understand very well. But perhaps it is not as important as he thinks.
BÉATRICE, surprised. : You of all people say that?
WERNER : You say conscience. But I call it fear instead.
BÉATRICE, quickly. : You know very well that Eustache is courageous.
WERNER : I agree. But that word has more than one meaning.
BÉATRICE : What do you mean by that?
WERNER : One can be brave before poverty, before danger, before death, but not before judgment.
BÉATRICE : What judgment, Werner?

WERNER : It is difficult to answer. I believe it is a mixture. Perhaps the idea that he himself forms of other people's judgment. But that idea comes from him. He thinks he doesn't care about people's opinion, and he also thinks he has nothing to blame himself for. But it is as if... in optics there is such a phenomenon. I do not know the name in French.
BÉATRICE : Interference?

WERNER : Probably. I do not know that word... I find that Eustache has changed enormously. Back in Germany in the old days... naturally he was not cheerful, but much calmer. He ate a lot, he drank a lot, we went on long walks in the countryside... It is so strange to see how he is now.
BÉATRICE : For me, in any case, it is exceedingly painful.
WERNER, moved. : But you bear no responsibility in that...
BÉATRICE : We have no children... For my part you can guess... But if I haven't even been capable of making him happy, or at least giving him a little serenity...

WERNER, with passion. : But it is not your fault... (Béatrice shakes her head; it is evident that she is keeping silent so as not to burst into tears.) Gisela is right, I don't think enough about what I say... I am clumsy. When I was a child, my mother never allowed me to touch fragile objects; I broke them every time without meaning to. You see, I haven't changed... What should I do? Naturally, perhaps I am mistaken. It must also be said that he works so hard. All those papers to grade, those articles he writes regularly in Le Nouveau Monde... I suppose he is tired...

BÉATRICE : If you only knew all that I hoped for when we were married! You can well imagine the situation was rather difficult. My parents didn't oppose it; my father has very broad views, my mother... resigned herself. But we didn't belong to the same background at all. I don't need to dwell on that. At bottom it doesn't matter anyway. But at the beginning I had to make great allowances. I was so sure that everything would work out in the end. But now... I am no longer so convinced.
WERNER, insincerely. : You are imagining things. There is no drama in that.

BÉATRICE : I have often noticed that in life what is most dreadful never leads to drama. The worst is what leads nowhere. I don't know, it's like those streets that lose themselves in wastelands on the outskirts of big cities. It seems to me sometimes that our lives are like those barely built avenues where no one ever walks, named after some forgotten city councilman...
WERNER, smiling. : You don't make me think of a city councilman.
BÉATRICE : Deep down, if I had been less selfish... no, I shouldn't say it.
WERNER : You are not selfish. You think only of Eustache.
BÉATRICE : Perhaps not in the way I should, since you can see very well that I am not helping him.
WERNER : It is clear that he cannot do without you.

BÉATRICE : I am sometimes haunted by a truly painful thought, Werner. I wonder whether for Eustache I don't embody something he would like to forget; yes, something he needs to turn his mind away from. That very success, that derisory success that embitters him like a failure. I cannot explain how I could have confided this impression to you—an impression I can barely admit to myself.
WERNER : I think it is because I am a foreigner.
BÉATRICE, after a silence. : You are right. To a French woman friend—and male friends I have none—it would have been impossible for me to say what you have just heard. But why?
WERNER : I cannot explain it. But it is obvious. (A silence.)
BÉATRICE : And yet I had no right to. And now it is as though...
[SCENE IV]
THE SAME, EUSTACHE.
EUSTACHE : What the devil! Are you both deaf, then? The telephone has been ringing for a quarter of an hour. (He picks up the receiver.) Naturally, nothing now.
BÉATRICE : I assure you, the ringer isn't loud enough.
EUSTACHE : What a joke! I can hear it from my study.
BÉATRICE : They will probably call back in a second.
EUSTACHE : I wonder what on earth you could have been saying to each other that was so absorbing... Eh?
BÉATRICE : It would be quite impossible for me to repeat it to you...
EUSTACHE : Why?
BÉATRICE : What about you, Werner?
WERNER : We were speaking... of Germany.
EUSTACHE : Oh really?
WERNER : Your wife was asking me questions. (The telephone rings.)
EUSTACHE, on the phone. : Hello! Yes, speaking. What? The Minister's office? Very well; I'll hold.
BÉATRICE, in an undertone, to Werner. : That's not right. You mustn't do that again.

EUSTACHE : Oh no, listen, please... Hello! Is that Monsieur Soreau himself on the line?... What do you say?... No, that is news to me... I assure you that I took no steps in that direction... Certainly... in principle... I am very touched... Thank you. Good day, sir. (He hangs up.)
BÉATRICE : What is it?
EUSTACHE : There's talk of appointing me to replace Fayet at Henri-IV.
BÉATRICE, pleased. : Oh?
EUSTACHE : It isn't done yet; they asked me not to talk about it. But it seems I stand the best chance.
BÉATRICE : What wonderful news!
WERNER : I congratulate you.
EUSTACHE, bitterly. : The marshal's baton.
BÉATRICE : You always told me that in your eyes it was the finest post in secondary education.
EUSTACHE : Exactly.
BÉATRICE : And besides, that is where you did your studies.
EUSTACHE : It's called coming full circle. Only... it's not yet settled that I'll accept.
BÉATRICE : What?
EUSTACHE : And it is even quite likely that I won't accept.
BÉATRICE : On what pretext?
EUSTACHE : No need for a pretext.
BÉATRICE : For what reason then?
EUSTACHE : First of all, I'd like to know who intervened on my behalf.
BÉATRICE : There was probably no need for any intervention. Your credentials were quite enough.
EUSTACHE : Don't make me laugh.
WERNER : In any case, what difference does it make to you? It's proof that you have good friends.
EUSTACHE : That's all I have, in fact. Only, you see, a man who hasn't even found a way to get himself thoroughly detested is a good-for-nothing. (A silence. Béatrice exits after nodding to Werner.)
[SCENE V]
EUSTACHE : I've been thinking about what you said earlier: it makes no sense at all. I cannot accept that you resign yourself so easily to the monstrous injustices displayed everywhere.
WERNER : What difference does it make whether I resign myself or not?
EUSTACHE : Art, joy, beauty—what do I know? We'll see to all that later. First, people have to eat. You don't seem to realize...
WERNER : Allow me to tell you, that is really rather rich; I am well enough placed to know that there is no justice.
EUSTACHE : You don't have, I think, the attitude your situation calls for.
WERNER : Explain.
EUSTACHE : I don't feel any revolt in you.

WERNER : That is to say, one would have to utter certain ritual words, I suppose. My thoughts ought to put on a uniform: the uniform of the outcast? But I detest uniforms, even that one. Above all, one must remain a man.
EUSTACHE : A man! A man! A word you seem to relish rolling around in your mouth... Speaking of Rudolf...
WERNER : I prefer not to speak of Rudolf right now.
EUSTACHE : Why? (Werner makes an evasive gesture.) He had a doctrine; he served a cause, he had committed himself...
WERNER : That is a word that frightens me.
EUSTACHE : People claim that the French are individualists...
WERNER : I do not know if that is still true.
EUSTACHE : I have never seen anyone who is to the degree that you are.
WERNER : It is always easy to stick on a label.
EUSTACHE : Whether you were conscious of it or not, the fact of leaving Germany classified you. You took a stand. One must still conform to the logic of one's actions.
WERNER : What logic?
EUSTACHE : You seem to refuse to make contact with the refugees who are in Paris; it's as if you didn't trust them.
WERNER : It's a question of personality. Besides, in general, I do not know them.
EUSTACHE : It's as though you were keeping to yourself. What the devil! Solidarity is a real thing.
WERNER : You are right, I am distrustful.
EUSTACHE : That is not a feeling you have any reason to be proud of, believe me.
WERNER : You are funny, Eustache! You get angry as if it were a personal matter.
EUSTACHE : I am not getting angry. I am asking to understand. I detest ambiguity. It's as if you couldn't bring yourself to burn your bridges with the people back there.
WERNER : You are mistaken.
EUSTACHE : Prove it to me.

WERNER : I burned them, no later than last night. There was a fellow who wrote to me, a man named Wetzinger whom I once knew in Berlin. A sort of impresario. He was also a journalist. I made an appointment to meet him in a café. I had a strong suspicion he was a scoundrel. Today, I know it.
EUSTACHE : What did he want from you?

WERNER : You see, he was an emissary. Nothing else. He began by talking about trifles. And then he showed his hand. He told me I was an idiot to stay here; that if I made certain written promises, I could return to Germany tomorrow, that they wouldn't bother me on account of Rudolf. He knew everything about me and about Gisela too. I don't even understand how those people are so well informed. Anyway, I don't care. I sent him packing, him and his proposals.
EUSTACHE : Did he make you concrete offers?
WERNER : And how! He guaranteed that I would be engaged at a theater, perhaps in Magdeburg or Dessau, or somewhere like that. And I know they were not just empty words.
EUSTACHE : How did he take your refusal?
WERNER : He said I was an idiot; that I would pay for my foolishness; that I was a traitor, and all that...
EUSTACHE : Did you tell your wife about this conversation?
WERNER, categorically. : Absolutely not. She will never know a thing. I beg of you not to make the slightest allusion in front of her to what I have told you.
EUSTACHE : Would she disapprove of you?
